text_translated_detailed: Page 1. Amboina, the 15th of May 1735. Register of Such Letters, Attachments and Other Papers as were sent to His Excellency the Well-Born and Highly Esteemed Lord Jacob Mossel, General of the Infantry in the service of the state of the United Netherlands, as well as Governor-General and the Well-Esteemed Lords Councillors of the Dutch Indies by order of the Esteemed and Highly Esteemed Lord Gerardus Cluijsenaar, Governor and Director of this province together with the Council, by the ships The Heir Prince and The House at Manpat to Batavia, namely from Amboina on the 15th of May 1738. This Register contains 90 items. No. 1. Original letter to the Highly Esteemed Government of today's date. 2. Copy of Resolutions of this Castle from the 14th of September of the previous year up to the 10th of this month. 3. Outgoing and incoming letters to and from the outer Comptoirs [trading posts] from the 7th of September of the previous year. 4. Incoming letters up to the last of April of the current year. 5. Five copies of Nagul Reports. 6. Copy of description of the Nagul trees. 7. Three copies of sworn Reports of the extirpated spice trees. 8. Copy of declaration regarding a slave who died in the quarter. 9. Account of what occurred on the Hongi expedition and at the Comptoirs [trading posts] Bouro and Manipa. 10. text_translated_detailed:
"The ship De Erf Prinsen, the duplicate per the ship Het Huijs de Manpat, arrived at Amboina on the 15th of May 1755. To Batavia. To His Excellency, the well-born, greatly esteemed Lord Jacob Mossel, General of the Infantry in the service of the state of the United Netherlands, as well as Governor-General and the worthy gentlemen, noble Councillors of the Dutch East Indies. Most noble, well-born, strict, greatly esteemed, valiant, wise, prudent, and most generous Lord and Lords.

On the 14th of February last, there arrived here by way of Grisse and Surabaya the ship De Erf Prins, and the following day directly the Pantchallang De Peperthuijn. The letters and papers received from Amboina on the 15th of May 1755, last under the guidance of letters dated the 10th of December of the year before last, as well as on the 14th of March thereafter, the ship Het Huijs te Manpat, with which two ships we have had the honor of receiving both in original and in duplicate your Excellency's most esteemed writings of the 31st of December of the past year, together with such enclosures and goods as the register and bill of lading and invoice came to show, being further handed over to us on the 12th of April by the Chinese Rhouwhianko the duplicate of your Excellency's letter of the 18th of February of this year, together with the judgment against the former violent offender Jan Dirk Boekemeijer, the executioner Jan Cornelis van der Land, and the native woman Andjella Lopis, all to our obligation and grateful acknowledgment, both for the favorable assistance in general as well as the accommodation and approval in particular of virtually all our actions in the year before last, as well as for the favorable permission to license yearly a certain number of Chialoupen [small boats] from private individuals for the purpose of fetching rice and other necessities for the Ambonese community to Makassar, which we at their departure in particular nothing

text_translated_detailed: General letter written by the Noble and Highly Esteemed Gentlemen the Seventeen in the Fatherland to Your Highly Esteemed Excellencies the Governor-General and the Council of India at Batavia, dated 8 October 1753, containing the matter of Amboina, which was as unwelcome to us as it appeared that this Government in the year 1751 had delivered only a very small quantity of merely 120,179 pounds of nutmeg, of which Your Excellencies had judged that half, and thus 60,000 pounds, could only be sent to the Netherlands and the other half had to be retained for Indian consumption. So welcome was it, on the other hand, to learn that the same in the future would deliver fairly larger quantities of this spice crop between the Offices of Hila and Laricque and nutmeg, though these were not picked here for their ripeness and could not be transported. What would it yield? Indeed, the nutmeg crop for the year 1752 was well calculated to amount to 1,219,900 pounds, which upon its arrival was found to fall short of expectations. We doubt whether, with the preservation of the ships (God willing), we shall receive at least two-thirds thereof and thus be in a position, by means of further considerable harvests, to lay up so much that we shall within a short time be able to proceed again to the previous old method of delivery. Meanwhile, upon receipt of such an unprecedented meager quantity of merely 60,000 pounds, some consolation was given by the later receipt of such an unprecedented meager quantity of still more than 26,000 pounds for the chambers Zeeland and Delft. However, because that entire quantity, in proportion to previous years and calculated according to the Fatherland's consumption, remained very small, the price in the following year's sale rose to 163 to 167 stuivers [modern equivalent: Dutch currency unit] per pound. Finally, I request that Your High Excellency would be so kind as to allow me to reside in Batavia, since the Government on Amboina may not regard me with favorable eyes, and that at the same time, during my absence here, I may be favored with greater income in order to be able to live, together with some more butter, oil, candles, and spices; since with one hundred and fifty reals I cannot subsist at all. Finally, I offer as a token of life a small writing case with silver mounting. Written on the 19th of April 1755. /Below/ For the translation /was signed/ E. W. Gordon. Register

High and well-born, Strict, Great and Esteemed: Manly, wise, provident, very Generous Lord and Lords. text_translated_detailed: having been summarized in our meeting of the 8th of this month, we found no significant problems therein, except some overly generous provisions, which we deemed good should be reimbursed by those to whom it falls to clear the writing offices of extraordinary expenses. From Ambon on September 26th, 1755. The offices of trade and soldier's pay, which of the houses to be kept rented, coming to damage in the year, although they were well restored and service was performed therein, have become completely unusable again through this earthquake, so that one has had to rent houses in the city for them, just as in the year past, which for the secretariat continues to this day, because the rooms or offices in the Castle could not be well repaired. Some repair money, since the carpentry and repairs to fortification works and buildings by Your Highness's now recently in the year 1753, by the drafted Memoir of His Excellency for the discussion of the state and interest of the Honored Company, at the offices has been determined to a certain sum, brought forward a question in our meeting of February 6th of this year by the aforementioned chief administrator, on what account the repairs already made and still to be made caused by the earthquake should be brought and written off, so as not to cause the determination of ordinary work to be significantly exceeded, so it was deemed good, following the example of the year 1695, to grant a qualification, so that all of it, as caused by an extraordinary cause, should also be written off to extraordinary carpentry and repairs. The Company's Chialoupen [small boats], in this province consist of three, of which the employment, the cruising, by the sides, from Ambon on May 8th, 1755, tin only in three poorly situated, as the Brigantine the Company's Chialoupje the Disobedience, the Chialoupje the Peace and the Pantjallang [boat names], the Pepper Brigantine, which two first-mentioned small vessels found their employment with the hauling of the Nagulen, timber works nearby, lime, etc. from the outer offices and the last with the cruising of Ceram's Coast, as this is known from a list going under the attachments, of which three vessels we, according to our resolution of the 8th of this month, have been forced to lay the Brigantine the Disobedience (on account of the heavy repairs required thereon and not well feasible here) until the last shipment, which small vessel, after it shall have been restored from its defects, we humbly request that we be sent back as soon as possible, together with such two Chialoupen as a two-masted and a one-masted, which Your Highness has been pleased to promise us for two years ago on the shown high necessity, particularly with an opulent Nagul harvest, so that we may be enabled in the month of December or the beginning of January next to have the Nagulen from the offices hauled away, for which otherwise we shall be completely unable, as that aforementioned resolution of the 8th of this month shows in more detail. The cruising south of Ceram's Coast, Ceram undertaken. Renovation of the placards [official notices/regulations]. From Ambon on September 26th, 1755.

text_translated_detailed: Concerning the 5th Translation Malay petition letter by the former King of Bantam Moel Fratah Mochamad Sifah Dzeinoel Ariefien To Amboina To His Excellency The High Noble great honorable Lord Jacob Mossel Governor General of Dutch India received at Batavia the 28 August 1755. This petition letter was sent in all submission with manifold greetings by the Sultan Aboel Fatah Mochamad Sifah Dzeinoel Ariefien residing at Amboina, to the High Noble great honorable Lord Jacob Mossel Governor General of Dutch India, to whom is wished continuing health and long life in his high esteemed dignity. Furthermore your High Nobility's humble Servant requests O that the same would be pleased to request on my behalf from the present King of Bantam the restitution of all such goods as my father the Sultan Aboel Moehasien Mochamad Dzeinoel Abiedien during his lifetime bequeathed for my portion, which was done with full consent of the Honored Lord Director Westpalm and the Honored Lord Bl om/ Amboina under date From which at that time were present at Bantam. / as well as the following persons: the State administrator Pangeeran Aria Poerba Nagara, the High Priests learned in law Pangeeran Aria Kalie Lamsoedien, the Priests ki Panghulu Abdoel Kadier, ki Panghulu Maas Sardjoodien Ki Panghulu Hadje Mansoer, together with the assembled brothers and sisters, own mother, and stepmothers likewise uncles and the further great and small state persons, having from the aforementioned inheritance by the blessing of the Almighty drawn the income for sixteen years. Requesting that His Excellency all the hereinafter named krises, pikes, and cutlasses together with further ammunition as becoming, would be pleased to have sold and the proceeds thereof sent. As firstly Cki Naga, ki moendarang, ki sitapak 1 piece kris called L ki Patoeroen, and kie Djiemat 3„ pikes —: Ki pantjoera,

text_translated_detailed: Subsequently, my eldest brother named Pangaran Ratoe Mochamad Saleh has bequeathed during his lifetime as a memorial a kris named Si Missam, 1 pike named Ki Djiemat, together with some ammunition, namely some small cannon pieces, and also some three-barreled muskets and flintlock guns. Goods belonging to his own property, namely 3 pieces of gold betel boxes, 1 box with filigree work, 12 diamond rings, table stones, 2 ring bracelets, each set with 7 diamond stones, 1 sunflower [ornament], 1 piece of gold bowl with its lids and piercings, filigree work, 1 piece with its fork and lid enameled, 1 gold beaker with its feet, 1 piece of gold small boxes, filigree work, 1 piece of gold betel boxes, 1 piece of silver betel box with filigree work, 3 chairs entirely covered with gold, 3 gold bonnets with filigree work, 3 packages of princely bridegroom's clothing with their respective head ornaments, 1 piece of silver betel box, a ring set with a garnet stone, small ornaments, together with the clothing of those who wear the ornaments. From Amboina under date 1755, 1 piece of sea clapper or betel set with its lacquered foot, 1 lacquered betel box spittoon, 1 silver lamp in the fashion of a bird, 1 lacquered ink container, 2 glass crowns, 12 pieces of candelabras, 2 pieces of glass lamps and their glass balls, Japanese, 1 piece of gold betel set with snake-head handles, 1 piece with some diamond-set [items]. Now proceeding to the income from the lands, namely: First, the forest, real Spanish dollars in cash 500. Tjiering brings in 25 takaar [a unit of measurement] clapper oil, each takaar 15 cans, comes to 26½ cans. The mountain Panimbang brings in yearly 500 Spanish dollars. Tjieboengoer the same. Tjarita the same. Anjar the same. Passa-ourang the same. Bombang the same.

The following mountain peoples of Djasinga [Jasinga] consist of:
Coppen - 1500
Soegoeheran - 1200

The villages Mandjaija and Tangaran are strong - 3000

And all of them pay individually, namely:
Married men: three reals Spanish [modern equivalent: Spanish silver coins] per year
Unmarried male persons: one real Spanish per year

A certain piece of land called Bogoor [Bogor], where 3000 Coppen are located, which yields 150 bundles of rice per year each.
